genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: the future barge pilot grew up beside a waterway
as a child she watched the boatmen tie their vessels to the quay
she began her working life as a helper on a sand barge
she learned to read the movement of the current
her training covered approach and slowing maneuvers
she learned to bring a heavy hull alongside despite the wind
after many seasons she was given command of a convoy
that convoy could tow two more craft
she now teaches the trade to beginners
she tells them to think ahead to the next maneuver
text: The woman who would one day pilot a barge grew up in a cluster of houses along a narrow canal. As a child she watched the boatmen tie their vessels to the quay and push off again at dawn toward the next lock. In her teens she took a helper's job aboard a barge loaded with sand, and there she learned to read the current. Her training was demanding. She had to master the approach, slow down without scraping the bank, and lay a heavy hull alongside while a crosswind shoved against it. After many seasons on the water she was given command of a full convoy, one that could tow two more craft behind it. She teaches beginners now, and she repeats a single rule to them: a careful boat handler is already thinking about the next maneuver, because water forgives nothing done in haste.

units: a funicular now serves a very steep slope
a winding road used to provide that link
the climb now costs travelers less effort
the shops at the top of the slope draw more customers
ridership runs past what the operators forecast
the cars are packed at peak times
the wait at the foot of the slope turns some users away
dropping the road shuttles leaves isolated residents without service
the installation is judged sound technically but badly sized
text: The funicular put in on the hillside deserves a mixed verdict. Its car climbs a steep face that a winding road used to serve, and swapping one for the other has pulled in two directions at once. Since the climb now costs a traveler no effort at all, the small shops at the top of the slope draw customers they had given up on, and their takings have risen sharply. Ridership, though, has run so far past what the operators forecast that the cars leave packed through the afternoon peak, and the line building up at the foot of the slope turns away part of the crowd, who give up and stay below. One more consequence is still argued over: the road shuttles were dropped, and the residents living farthest out have no service at all. The engineering side convinces. The sizing plainly does not.

units: the writer of the message moved far from where he works
his coach trip took a very long time
traffic jams made the arrival time impossible to predict
he arrived worn out before he had even started
a coworker suggested a combined solution to him
he now reaches the station with a folding bike
he finishes the trip on a regional train
the bike lets him get around heavy traffic
he saves half a period on his old run
he invites the person he is writing to come try the route
text: You asked whether the move had wrecked everything, and at first, honestly, it had. The coach crawled, it sat behind a line of cars that never seemed to end, and I could never tell what minute I would walk in. I would show up worn out before starting anything at all. Then a coworker floated an idea I should have come up with myself: split the trip in two. Now I head out with a folding bike, slip past the stopped traffic all the way down to the station, and finish on a regional train, where I finally get to sit with the bike tucked under the seat. The run is half a period shorter than the old one, and I turn up cheerful instead of furious. Rain is the one drawback, but a cape handles it. Come out some morning and I will lend you the spare bike, and you can ride the route with me.

units: a planning specialist answers a reporter's questions
she compares the streetcar and the bus with a reserved lane
the streetcar carries more riders on each run
rails call for costly and lengthy works
the bus goes into service far more quickly
the bus copes badly with heavy crowds
the streetcar keeps its edge on very busy corridors
she warns against deciding without studying local demand
she holds the route to matter more than the type of vehicle
text: Lay down track, or paint a reserved lane? We put that question to a specialist in the planning of large towns. The two options never come out even, she answers, and it is the setting that decides between them. A streetcar takes on far more riders at each run, she explains, and it moves along without getting stuck behind the general traffic. Against that, laying rail means a heavy, expensive worksite, one that ties up the streets for whole seasons at a time. A bus in a protected lane goes into service quickly and can be shifted elsewhere if the demand moves, but it chokes as soon as the flows begin to swell. On the busiest corridors, then, the streetcar keeps its edge. Her conclusion refuses any clean verdict. Before you pick a vehicle, she says, study what the demand really is, because a badly drawn route ruins whatever runs on it.

units: a woman traveling asks a sailor a question on the deck of a night ferry
the sailor lists what he loves about his work
he names the smell of wet rope
he mentions the noise of the chains being worked
he brings up the brightness of the markers on dark water
he values the quiet of the sleeping passengers
he says he knows the regulars by their walk
he claims the crossing home never resembles the crossing out
text: On the deck of the night ferry, a woman traveling alone asked the sailor what still held him to the work. He rested a hand on the rail and answered her with a list, as though he had had it ready for a long while. He loved the smell of wet rope, he said, that thick scent which soaks into your palms and stays there. He loved the clatter of the chains being worked before a landing, a racket that announces the shore ahead. He loved the brightness of the markers set out on black water, told off one by one all the way to the mouth of the channel. He loved the quiet of the passengers dozing against their bags under scratchy blankets. He knew the regulars by nothing more than their careful step on the wet plating. And before he went back up to the bridge again, he added that the crossing home never once resembles the crossing out.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: the first heavy loads were moved on wooden rollers
the invention of the spoked wheel made vehicles lighter
a harness bearing on the shoulders replaced the strap that pressed on the animals' throats
that change raised the pulling force available
roads laid with broken stone kept the wheels from sinking
wooden strips then guided the carts in the mines
steam removed the dependence on animal strength
each advance worked on the contact between the vehicle and the ground
text: Before any machinery existed at all, shifting a heavy mass meant levering it onto wooden rollers and carrying each roller back around to the front, over and over. The spoked wheel came later and made the bodies of vehicles lighter, so that far less effort went into getting them moving. Then the harness changed, and that mattered more than it sounds: the strap that pressed on an animal's throat gave way to a collar bearing on the shoulders, and teams could suddenly pull loads that had been well out of reach. Roads were laid with broken stone so that the rims stopped sinking down into mud. In the mine galleries, wooden strips were set down to guide the carts along their run. Steam closed the sequence out by cutting the tie to muscle. Each step worked on the same weak point, the place where the vehicle meets the ground.

units: a slowdown can appear with no obstacle and no crash
one driver brakes lightly for some small reason
the driver behind brakes harder out of caution
the amplification travels back down the line
the line ends up stopping completely
the wave of slowing moves backward while the cars go forward
keeping enough room ahead of you softens the effect
following too closely makes the spread worse
text: It happens that a line of cars comes to a standstill although no obstacle and no crash of any kind blocks the roadway ahead. The mechanism behind it can be described exactly. One driver eases off the pedal for some small reason: a clumsy merge, a glance away, a rise in the road. The driver behind him sees the brake lights come on and presses a good deal harder, out of caution. The third reacts more sharply still, and the gaps go on tightening. Step by step the amplification travels back up the column until cars a long way behind have to stop dead. The odd part is that this wave of slowing moves backward through the line while the cars themselves keep rolling forward. The remedy fits into a single instruction: keep a comfortable gap ahead of you, and never ride the bumper of the driver in front.

units: a coach of hikers turns onto a mountain track
a rockfall blocks the road above a ravine
the width of the passage rules out turning around
the driver refuses to back down through several bends
the passengers clear away the lighter stones
a farm tractor arrives from the settlement nearby
the tractor pulls the main block aside with a chain
the trip starts again with a modest delay
the woman driving the tractor refuses any payment
text: The hikers' coach had turned onto a stony track that wound its way up toward the pass. Coming out of a bend that overhung a ravine, they found fallen rock lying right across the roadway. The track was far too narrow to turn on, and the driver flatly refused to back down over that many bends on so rough a surface. The passengers climbed out and cleared away the lighter stones by hand, but the largest one would not shift at all, however hard they pushed at it. A farmer from the settlement below finally appeared with her tractor, ran a chain around the block of rock, and dragged it onto the shoulder in three unhurried pulls. The coach set off again with only a modest delay, and the whole group applauded. Asked to name her price, she shrugged, climbed back up, and drove down toward her barns.

units: the text explains how to choose between a night train and a long-distance coach
it advises comparing the price of the two options first
the night train saves you paying for a room
the coach reaches stops the railway skips
the reader should check the arrival time before booking
booking a berth away from the corridor is recommended
you have to bring a soft bag for want of storage space
the coach forces stops that break up your sleep
the final choice rests on how much you value rest
text: Torn between a night train and a long-distance coach? Work through it in order. Compare the fares first, but add to the ticket price what a room would have cost you, because the train often makes up the difference that way. Then look at the map of stops, since the coach reaches small towns that the railway skips entirely. Check the arrival time before you book, or you will land before the ticket windows open. If you go by rail, pick a berth away from the corridor and bring a soft bag, or you will sleep against your luggage with your knees folded up. If you take the road, accept in advance the required stops that will wake you in the dark, and pack something to cover your eyes. Then settle it with one question: do you want to arrive rested, or to pay as little as you can?

units: a report describes an abandoned rail line being put back in service
crews have replaced the rotted ties
a tunnel overrun by roots has been cleared
a footbridge has been added for cyclists
people living nearby dread the noise of trains after dark
local growers count on shipping their goods by rail
riders will try the line before it officially opens
the fares have not been settled yet
text: Rusted rails that the brush had been swallowing up for a whole generation are carrying trains once more. Our report from the site of the reopening holds on to several points. The track comes first: crews have pulled out the rotted ties and cleared a tunnel where the roots had grown down as far as the ballast. Access comes next: a steel footbridge now spans the cutting, so that cyclists no longer have to scramble down the embankment to reach the far side. Then come the worries, since people living nearby dread the rumble of trains after dark and are asking for sound barriers. And the hopes, last of all: growers around the area are counting on shipping their harvests by rail. Riders will travel the line before it officially opens. The fare table, for its part, has not been settled yet.
